section.title: Create in Me a Clean Heart
section.sectionRationale: David's great penitential psalm, written after Nathan the prophet confronted him over his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah. It is the model of biblical repentance: honest confession, a plea not merely for pardon but for a new heart, and a resolve to praise and teach others, anticipating the new heart promised in the new covenant.
section.thesis: David's honest confession after his sin with Bathsheba models true repentance, casting himself wholly on God's mercy and pleading not just for pardon but for a new heart, a prayer fully answered in the new covenant and the Spirit poured out through Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the plea for mercy and confession of sin reaching back to birth; the central prayer for a clean heart and a right spirit; the vow to teach transgressors and offer a broken and contrite heart; and a closing prayer for the good of Zion.

units.label: Have mercy on me, O God
units.note: the plea and confession of inbred sin

verses.text: Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your {{chesed|loving devotion}}; according to Your great compassion, blot out my transgressions.
Wash me clean of my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin.
For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me.
Against You, You only, have I sinned and done what is evil in Your sight, so that You may be proved right when You speak and blameless when You judge.
Surely I was brought forth in iniquity; I was sinful when my mother conceived me.
Surely You desire truth in the inmost being; You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.

units.label: Create in me a clean heart, O God
units.note: the central prayer for cleansing and renewal

verses.text: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean; wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
Let me hear joy and gladness; let the bones You have crushed rejoice.
Hide Your face from my sins and blot out all my iniquities.
{{bara|Create}} in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right {{ruach|spirit}} within me.
Cast me not away from Your presence; take not Your Holy Spirit from me.
Restore to me the joy of Your salvation, and sustain me with a willing spirit.

units.label: Then I will teach transgressors Your ways
units.note: the vow to praise and teach

verses.text: Then I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You.

Deliver me from bloodguilt, O God, the God of my salvation, 
and my tongue will sing of Your righteousness.
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth will declare Your praise.
For You do not delight in sacrifice, or I would bring it; You take no pleasure in burnt offerings.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and a contrite heart, 
O God, You will not despise.

units.label: Build up the walls of Jerusalem

verses.text: In Your good pleasure, cause Zion to prosper; build up the walls of Jerusalem.

Then You will delight in righteous sacrifices, in whole burnt offerings; 
then bulls will be offered on Your altar.

chesed.gloss: Steadfast, covenant loving devotion. David's opening plea rests entirely on this quality of God's character, not on any merit of his own, appealing to the same loving devotion that grounds every promise of mercy in Scripture.

bara.gloss: To create, specifically the verb used in Genesis 1:1 for God's creation from nothing. David does not ask God merely to repair or improve his heart but to bara, to create something wholly new, as radical as the first creation itself.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. David prays for a right ruach within him and pleads that God's Holy Spirit not be taken from him, language that anticipates the Spirit given permanently to God's people under the new covenant.

basic.context: This is David's prayer after Nathan the prophet confronted him over his adultery with Bathsheba and his arrangement of her husband Uriah's death, 2 Samuel 11 to 12. David does not make excuses. He confesses his sin as against God above all, admits that sin runs all the way down to his very nature, and pleads not merely for forgiveness but for an entirely new heart and a right spirit within him.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm is meant to be prayed, not just studied. It is widely regarded as the model of true repentance in Scripture: honest, undefended confession that moves beyond regret over consequences to sorrow over sin against God, and beyond mere pardon to a longing for inner transformation.
basic.originalLanguages: David appeals to God's chesed, His covenant loving devotion, as the sole ground of mercy. His central plea, bara, create in me a clean heart, uses the same verb for God's creation from nothing in Genesis 1:1, and he begs that God's ruach, His Holy Spirit, not be withdrawn from him.
basic.typology: The hyssop and cleansing David describes point forward to the true cleansing accomplished by Christ's blood. His plea for a new heart and a right spirit anticipates the new covenant promise of a new heart and God's own Spirit placed within His people.
basic.christ: The cleansing David seeks with hyssop, verse 7, foreshadows the true cleansing of conscience accomplished by the blood of Christ, Hebrews 9:13-14, 1 John 1:7. His plea, create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit, anticipates the new covenant promise of a new heart and God's Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27, fulfilled in the new birth Jesus describes in John 3:3-8. David's bloodguilt, incurred through Uriah's murder, is answered ultimately by the innocent blood of Christ shed for the guilty.
basic.god: God is both perfectly just, so that His judgment is right even when it falls on His own anointed king, and abundantly merciful, ready to create a clean heart and restore the joy of salvation to the truly repentant. He does not delight in ritual sacrifice divorced from a broken and contrite heart.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Samuel 12:1-13 records the historical events behind this psalm, Nathan's confrontation and David's confession. Ezekiel 36:26-27 promises a new heart and God's Spirit within His people. Hebrews 9:13-14 shows Christ's blood cleansing the conscience far beyond any Old Testament ritual.
basic.oneStory: David's honest confession and plea for a new heart is the model of repentance for every sinner. That plea is answered fully in Christ, whose blood cleanses what hyssop only pictured, and whose Spirit creates the clean heart David could only pray for, poured out on all who trust Him under the new covenant.

context.literary:
Psalm 51 is built on a plain progression: confession, cleansing, renewal, and a vow. The opening two verses lay out a full vocabulary of sin and forgiveness. Three words for wrong are stacked, transgression, iniquity and sin, verses 1 to 3, and three verbs for removal answer them, blot out, wash and cleanse. Transgression is rebellion, iniquity is what is crooked or twisted, and sin is missing the mark. David does not reach for the lightest word. He uses all three, and gives each a remedy.

The centre of the psalm is the pivot from what God must do to what God must make. Up to verse 9 the verbs ask God to remove: blot out, wash, purify, hide His face. From verse 10 they ask God to give: create, renew, restore, sustain. The psalm is not content with a clean slate. It asks for a changed person to stand on it. The three references to spirit in verses 10 to 12, a right spirit, the Holy Spirit and a willing spirit, hold the second half together.

Verses 13 to 17 are conditional on that renewal, opening with 'Then I will teach', and the vow that follows is stated in terms of the mouth. David's mouth had been silent under guilt, and Psalm 32:3-5 gives the other side of that silence, bones brittle from groaning until he acknowledged his sin. Now he asks God to open his lips, verse 15. The psalm then reaches its statement on sacrifice, verses 16 and 17, in which he declines to offer what he cannot properly offer and names what God accepts.

The last two verses look wider, from one man's guilt to the city. Some treat them as a later liturgical addition and some as David's own; the question is taken up in the debates below. Either way, they place personal repentance inside the life of the covenant community, and end with the sacrifices of verse 19 restored to honor. The psalm begins with 'me' and ends with 'Zion'.
context.historical:
The heading ties the psalm to the confrontation recorded in 2 Samuel 12. David had taken Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and to hide the child he sent Uriah back to the front with a letter to Joab, 'Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle', 2 Samuel 11:15. Uriah died, and David waited out the mourning and took her as his wife. Nathan came with a parable of a poor man's ewe lamb, and David, angry, said the rich man 'deserves to die', 2 Samuel 12:5. Nathan answered, 'You are that man!', 2 Samuel 12:7.

David's reply was five words in Hebrew, and Nathan's answer was immediate: 'The LORD has taken away your sin. You will not die', 2 Samuel 12:13. The Law knew a death penalty for adultery, Leviticus 20:10, and murder was no lighter. A king who could not be tried by any court in the land had nowhere to go but to God. That is part of what he means by 'Against You, You only'. Even so, the consequences did not lift. The sword would never leave his house, and the child born to Bathsheba died after seven days, while David fasted and lay on the ground, 2 Samuel 12:10, 15-18.

There was no ordinary sacrifice for the sin he had committed. The Law allowed offerings for unintentional sin, but the person who 'sins defiantly' was to be cut off, Numbers 15:30-31. David had sinned with a high hand, so the sacrificial system offered him no formula to follow. That explains why he says God takes no pleasure in burnt offerings, verse 16. There was nothing on the altar to fit his case, and he could rely on God's mercy alone.

The psalm has been prayed in the church for centuries, and the Western church numbered it among the seven penitential psalms, with Psalms 6, 32, 38, 102, 130 and 143. Its Latin opening word, Miserere, became the name of the psalm in the liturgy. Scripture never softens the story. Matthew's genealogy still says that David was the father of Solomon 'by Uriah's wife', Matthew 1:6, and 1 Kings 15:5 sums up his life as right in the eyes of the LORD 'except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite'.
context.canonical:
Psalm 51 is the fullest prayer of repentance in the Bible, and it draws on earlier texts to make its case. The three verbs of forgiveness in the opening lines are echoed by God's own word in Isaiah 43:25, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake', and by Isaiah 1:18, where sins like scarlet become white as snow, which David borrows for verse 7. Hyssop belongs to the cleansing rites for leprosy and for contact with the dead, Leviticus 14:4-6 and Numbers 19:18, and to the Passover blood on the doorframes, Exodus 12:22. David uses the language of ritual purity for a sin that ritual could not touch.

The psalm sits beside Psalm 32, which opens 'Blessed is he whose transgressions are forgiven', and the two are companion pieces: Psalm 32 looks back on the relief of confessing, Psalm 51 is the confession itself. Psalm 130:3-4 gives the theology beneath both: 'If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who, O Lord, could stand? But with You there is forgiveness.' Proverbs 28:13 states the rule that the one who confesses and renounces sin finds mercy.

The promises of a new heart and spirit in Ezekiel 36:25-27 and Ezekiel 11:19, and the law written on the heart in Jeremiah 31:33, reach for the very thing David asks in verses 10 to 12. In the New Testament, Paul quotes verse 4 in Romans 3:4, where he argues that God is true even if every man is a liar, and that He will be 'proved right when You speak'. Jesus tells of a tax collector who beat his breast and prayed 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner', Luke 18:13, in the spirit of verse 1, and the prodigal's 'I have sinned against heaven and against you', Luke 15:21, echoes verse 4. John 3:5 and Titus 3:5 speak of washing and renewal by the Spirit in terms that recall the psalm's cleansing and its request for a new spirit.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
David, or the psalm's later singers in his voice, meant Israel to hear how a forgiven sinner actually prays. The psalm makes no excuse and offers no explanation. It does not bring up Bathsheba's part or the pressures of a king's life, and it does not shift the blame. It moves at once to God's character, asking for mercy on the basis of His loving devotion and compassion rather than on the strength of David's regret. The first hearers were meant to see that repentance starts with an appeal to God's own nature, and they were meant to notice that the appeal is made by their king. Even the anointed leader stands under the word of the LORD.

The psalm also aims to correct a shallow view of forgiveness. Verses 5 and 6 show David tracing his act to a condition that lies deeper than the act. He does not use this as an excuse; it is why he knows he cannot repair himself, and why he asks for something to be made, verse 10. The hearers were to learn that outward acts of sorrow and ritual would not be enough, and that the only sacrifice God receives is a broken spirit, verse 17.

Finally the psalm is a promise about mission. The forgiven man will teach transgressors, verse 13, and sing of righteousness, verse 14. Mercy received is meant to become witness.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm is a prayer from a particular man in a particular crisis, and it does not tell every believer to expect the same sequence of events. It records David's confession and the requests he made. It does not promise that every repentant sinner will be spared consequences, and the narrative of 2 Samuel 12 shows that forgiveness and consequence can stand together: the sin was taken away, and the child still died. Readers should not treat David's fasting or his sackcloth as required rituals.

What carries over is the shape of the prayer. It is honest about the deed, it puts the offence against God first, it appeals to mercy alone, and it asks for a changed heart and not just relief. The verses on the Holy Spirit, verse 11, need care. David lived before Pentecost, and he prays out of the fear that God may remove His presence as He had from Saul, 1 Samuel 16:14. Christians who are in Christ are given the promise that the Spirit lives in them, Romans 8:9, so they can pray verse 11 as a plea for the joy of that presence and against sin's power to grieve the Spirit, Ephesians 4:30, but not in fear that the promise itself will be withdrawn.

debates.question: What does David mean by 'Against You, You only have I sinned'?

views.label: Sin is above all an offence against God
views.case: Every command comes from God, so every wrong breaks His law before it breaks a person. Nathan's word to David, 'you have despised the command of the LORD', 2 Samuel 12:9, and David's own 'I have sinned against the LORD', 2 Samuel 12:13, put the offence there. Joseph said the same when he refused Potiphar's wife, Genesis 39:9. The prodigal's confession is a model, Luke 15:21.

views.label: David speaks as a king answerable to no earthly court
views.case: As king, David had no human judge above him for what he did to Uriah and Bathsheba. There was nowhere to answer but to God. On this reading 'You only' is a legal statement as well as a spiritual one, and it does not deny the wrong done to Uriah.

views.label: A poetic sweep and not an absolute claim
views.case: Others hold that the Hebrew idiom marks a contrast, so that the sin was against God far more than against anyone else. Hebrew poetry often states a comparison as if it were an exclusion.

debates.bearing: All three agree that David is not trying to lessen his guilt toward Uriah. He is saying that the deepest wrong is what sin does to a person's standing before the Lord, and that is why only God's forgiveness can deal with it.

debates.question: What is verse 5 saying about human origins?

views.label: It teaches inherited sin
views.case: Augustine and the Reformers took the verse as one of the main biblical texts for original sin. Read beside Romans 5:12, where death came to all 'because all sinned', and Psalm 58:3, where the wicked are estranged 'from the womb', it says human nature is bent from the start. Job 14:4 asks who can bring out clean from unclean.

views.label: It is a personal confession that the sin runs deep
views.case: Others say David is speaking about himself with the strong language of poetry, meaning that he cannot remember a time when he was not prone to sin. On this view the verse does not claim that conception or birth is sinful in itself, and it says nothing about Bathsheba or about his mother.

views.label: It reflects the world into which he was born
views.case: Some Eastern traditions stress that we are born into a world of sin and death and are affected by it, without holding that guilt is passed on as the Western church taught.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the mechanism. What it does teach is that the root of sin lies below the level of single acts, which is why David asks for a heart to be created and not simply a deed to be forgiven.

debates.question: Are verses 18 and 19 David's or a later addition?

views.label: A later prayer from the exile
views.case: Verses 18 and 19 ask God to build the walls of Jerusalem, and in David's day the city was newly captured and not in ruins. Many scholars read the ending as an addition from the time of the Babylonian destruction, adapting a personal psalm for the community, as Nehemiah 2:17 shows the walls in ruins.

views.label: David's own closing prayer
views.case: Others say David was king and worried for the well being of the nation, and that his sin had put Zion in danger. Building up can also refer to strengthening or prosperity rather than repair after ruin, and verse 19 is a natural resolution of verses 16 and 17.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that verses 16 to 19 belong together. Verses 16 and 17 do not abolish sacrifice, since verse 19 promises that righteous offerings will again please God. The meaning is that offerings please Him when they come from a heart already broken and mended.

study.originalLanguages:
The verbs of the opening lines are chosen with care. To 'wash' in verse 2, and again in verse 7, is kabas, the verb for laundering cloth, used in Exodus 19:10 for the people washing their garments before Sinai. Blot out is machah, to wipe a written record, and the word God uses of Himself in Isaiah 43:25. David asks for stains to be scrubbed and the record erased.

In verse 7 'Purify me' is a form of the verb formed from the root for sin, and it carries the sense of removing sin, of un-sinning a person. Translators render it purify or cleanse. The image of hyssop in the same verse points to the bunch of plant used to sprinkle blood and water in the rites of Leviticus 14:4-6 and Numbers 19:18. What David says is that only God can do with a guilty conscience what the priest did with a leper: declare it clean and mean it.

Verse 8 has the bones God has 'crushed'. The Hebrew root is dakah, to crush or break in pieces, and the same root turns up in verse 17 in the word for a 'contrite' heart. The crushing God allowed in the bones in verse 8 is the same as the crushing of the heart He accepts in verse 17. Isaiah 53:5 uses this family of words of the servant, 'He was crushed for our iniquities'.

Verse 10 uses bara, 'create', with God as subject. Bara is used in the Old Testament only of God's activity. David is asking for something only God can do. The clean heart is a heart made tahor, the word for ritual and moral purity, and the 'right' spirit is a spirit made steady and firm, the sense of the Hebrew nakon. The word 'renew' belongs to the vocabulary of Isaiah 65:17, where God says He will 'create new heavens and a new earth'. Verse 12 adds a 'willing' spirit, one that is generous and ready of its own accord, so verses 10 to 12 gather three spirits, one steady, one holy and one willing, which are best read as three ways of describing the one life that God gives.

Verse 11 has the phrase 'Your Holy Spirit', which appears in the Old Testament only here and in Isaiah 63:10-11. There the people grieved the Holy Spirit and God became their enemy, and then they remembered the God who had set His Holy Spirit among them. David fears the same fate as Saul, from whom the Spirit of the LORD had departed, 1 Samuel 16:14.

Verse 14 asks to be delivered from 'bloodguilt'. The Hebrew is plural, literally bloods, and it is the standard phrase for the guilt of shed blood. Here it names the death of Uriah plainly, which David has avoided naming until now. The BSB footnote to verse 4 notes that the Septuagint reads 'victorious', and that Paul cites it that way in Romans 3:4. The Hebrew idea is that God is proved right in a legal sense, and the Greek is more like winning a case. In either wording, David wants God's verdict on him to be seen to be just.

typology.type: Hyssop and the cleansing rites, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Hyssop was dipped in the blood of the Passover lamb, Exodus 12:22, and used to sprinkle blood and water on the leper and on those touched by death, Leviticus 14:4-6 and Numbers 19:18. Hebrews compares those rites with the work of Christ: if the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer sanctify the unclean, 'how much more will the blood of Christ ... purify our consciences from works of death', Hebrews 9:13-14. The type could cleanse the body and mark the person as fit to worship, but it could not reach the conscience. Christ's blood does, and 1 John 1:7 says it cleanses from all sin.

typology.type: The broken and contrite heart as the acceptable sacrifice, verse 17
typology.fulfillment: David's broken spirit is the offering God does not despise, and Isaiah 57:15 and 66:2 say that God dwells with the contrite and esteems the humble. The Servant of Isaiah 53:5 was 'crushed for our iniquities', so the brokenness that David brings by way of repentance is met by a brokenness that Christ bore on behalf of sinners. Jesus' first beatitude, blessing the poor in spirit, matches the psalm. The type falls short because David's contrition does not itself pay for sin, and it is Christ's death that makes contrition acceptable.

typology.type: A new heart and a steady spirit, verses 10 to 12
typology.fulfillment: David asks for what the prophets promise to a whole people: 'I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you', Ezekiel 36:26, with God's Spirit put within them, Ezekiel 36:27. Jesus tells Nicodemus that no one can enter the kingdom without being born of water and the Spirit, John 3:5, and Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17, and 'created in Christ Jesus to do good works', Ephesians 2:10. David could pray for it and be given a measure of it. Under the new covenant it is the promise of every believer, and the Spirit is given to those who ask, Luke 11:13.

typology.type: David the king who sinned and was pardoned, verses 1 to 4
typology.fulfillment: David is the anointed son of Israel's line, and the psalm shows the failure of the best king they had. The covenant with David promised a son who would reign forever, and the Gospels name Jesus the son of David, in a genealogy that still includes 'Uriah's wife', Matthew 1:6. The pattern is a king who needs cleansing giving way to a King who is Himself without sin, Hebrews 4:15, and who cleanses His people. The type falls short because David can only plead for pardon. Christ gives it.

study.christ:
Psalm 51 shows the weight of the problem that Christ answers. David asks for something that no ritual in the Law could give him, a heart made clean. The question the psalm leaves is how a holy God can be 'proved right' when He forgives a murderer and adulterer. Paul's answer in Romans 3:21-26 is that God presented Christ as the place where mercy and justice meet, so that He is both just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. David's plea 'according to Your loving devotion' is heard in the light of the cross, where God's justice and mercy do not need to be balanced against each other.

The psalm's vocabulary is used of Christ's work again and again. David asks for the record to be blotted out, and Paul says God forgave us all our trespasses 'having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross', Colossians 2:13-14. David asks to be washed and made whiter than snow, and John writes that 'the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin', 1 John 1:7, and that if we confess, 'He is faithful and just to forgive us', 1 John 1:9. Hebrews 9:22 reminds us that 'without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness', which is why David's prayer, unlike his bulls and goats, is not the last word. It is a prayer that hoped for something the blood of animals could not supply, Hebrews 10:4.

David asks for a clean heart and God's Spirit to stay, and Jesus is the one who gives both. He tells Nicodemus that entrance to the kingdom requires birth 'of water and the Spirit', John 3:5, and on the evening of the resurrection He breathed on the disciples and said 'Receive the Holy Spirit', John 20:22. The Spirit David feared to lose is the Spirit Christ pours out on all who trust Him, so that His people can pray verse 12, 'sustain me with a willing spirit', as those already upheld.

The cross also answers the phrase 'bloodguilt'. David's guilt came from the shedding of an innocent man's blood. Jesus is the innocent man whose blood was shed on behalf of the guilty, Matthew 26:28. There is a bitter irony here: David had an innocent man killed in order to keep a guilty king safe, and God brought his own Son out of David's line to lay down His life for guilty kings and their subjects alike. A caution is needed. The psalm is not a coded prediction of Christ's suffering in every line. It is David's honest prayer, and the New Testament shows what God did to make such a prayer answerable.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 51 is the one who is right whichever way He judges. David says that God is 'blameless when You judge', verse 4, and he does not ask God to lower the standard. There is no bargaining in the psalm. The Law said death, and David does not say the law was too severe. The God he prays to is holy enough that David places himself entirely at His disposal, and merciful enough that David still dares to ask.

Mercy in this psalm rests on God's own character, and not on David's quality. David asks 'according to Your loving devotion' and 'according to Your great compassion', verse 1. Compassion here is the word for a mother's womb, the tender feeling that moves a person to pity. God is not stirred by David's merits, because there are none to plead. He is moved by who He is. Psalm 130:4 says that forgiveness is with Him so that He may be feared, and this is one of the psalm's quiet surprises. Forgiveness does not weaken awe. It deepens it.

God is also the creator, and the psalm makes this concrete by asking Him to create a clean heart, verse 10. A human being can turn over a new leaf, but only God can give a new heart. The psalm treats change as a work of God and not merely a product of resolve. It also portrays God as one who wants truth 'in the inmost being', verse 6, so He looks below the visible act to the place where motive and desire are formed. Jeremiah 17:9 says the heart is deceitful, and Mark 7:21-23 shows Jesus locating sin in the heart. In this psalm God reaches that place.

The verse on the Holy Spirit, verse 11, shows God present with a person in a way that can be lost from view and felt as absence. Saul's story, 1 Samuel 16:14, shows how serious it can be, and David's fear is real. The psalm therefore also shows God as the one who restores 'the joy of Your salvation', verse 12. He is the source of joy, and He restores it.

For worship, the psalm teaches that God does not receive an offering that is a substitute for the heart. He does not despise a broken spirit, verse 17, and Isaiah 57:15 says He dwells with the contrite. To worship Him well is to come as David did, empty handed, expecting only mercy, and to leave singing of His righteousness, verse 14.

crossReferences.note: The historical event behind the psalm. Nathan tells the story of the poor man's lamb, David condemns the rich man, and Nathan says 'You are that man'. The psalm should be read as David's answer to that moment, and 2 Samuel 12:13 records the first words of it: 'I have sinned against the LORD'.

David's other great psalm of forgiveness. It describes the physical and spiritual weight of unconfessed sin, bones brittle from groaning, and the relief that came on confessing. It is often read as the reflection after the prayer of Psalm 51 and shares its words for transgression, sin and iniquity.

The LORD invites sinners to reason with Him, promising that sins like scarlet will be as white as snow. David's cry that he will be 'whiter than snow', verse 7, borrows the image of a cleansing beyond what the stain would suggest, and rests on the same promise that God can make the guilty clean.

God says that He is the one who blots out transgressions for His own sake and remembers sins no more. The verb for blotting out is the one David uses in verses 1 and 9. It shows that the ground of forgiveness is God's own name, and it explains why David can appeal to His character.

The person who sins defiantly is cut off, having despised the word of the LORD. It explains why sacrifices could not help David, whose sin was high handed, and why verse 16 says there was no offering he could bring. Only mercy could reach a sin the sacrificial law could not cover.

God promises to sprinkle clean water, to give a new heart and a new spirit, and to put His own Spirit within His people. The passage reads as an answer to verses 7 to 12, for it pairs cleansing with renewal from within, and it looks ahead to the new covenant that David could only pray for.

Paul quotes verse 4, that God may be 'proved right when You speak and victorious when You judge', in his argument that God stays true even when every human is false. The apostle takes David's confession as a statement about God's justice which stands for all people.

The writer contrasts the blood of goats and bulls and the ashes of a heifer, which sanctified the body, with the blood of Christ, which purifies the conscience from works of death. It picks up the ritual language of hyssop and shows why the cleansing David asked for could finally come only through Christ.

John writes that the blood of Jesus cleanses us from all sin, and that if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to forgive. It is the New Testament counterpart of the psalm, showing the same pairing of cleansing and confession and stating the basis of it in Christ.

The Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul and a spirit of distress began to torment him. It gives the background to verse 11, where David begs that God's Holy Spirit not be taken from him, and shows that he had seen what it looked like when God's presence left a king.

God dwells in a high and holy place and also with the humble in spirit, to revive the heart of the contrite. It is a companion to verse 17, saying why a broken heart is not despised: the holy God has chosen to live with those who are crushed.

The tax collector stands at a distance, beats his breast and says 'God, have mercy on me, a sinner!' Jesus says he went home justified. It is a living picture of the psalm's first verse, and shows the pattern of David's prayer being taken up by an ordinary person and answered.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 51 asks a question that the whole Bible has already raised: what happens when the person made in God's image breaks His law, and can what has been done be undone? In Genesis 1:27 humanity was created in God's image, and in Genesis 3 sin enters. David's prayer names the result. Wrong is done against God, guilt sits in the conscience, the person is bent from the start, and the heart itself needs to be remade. The psalm returns to the creation vocabulary of the first chapter, asking God to 'create' what he cannot produce.

Its place in the story is at the height of the Davidic kingdom. God had promised David a house and a throne, and the same king fails at the point where the promise is strongest. The psalm shows that the covenant with David rests on God's mercy and not on David's record. The prophets later pick up the same themes: the God who blots out transgressions for His own sake, Isaiah 43:25, the God who will give a new heart and put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:26-27, and a covenant written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33. Psalm 51 is a prayer for that future, said in the present.

The gospel answers the prayer. A Son of David, Jesus, is born to the line that includes Uriah's wife, and He offers Himself for the guilty. On the cross the debt is canceled, Colossians 2:14, the conscience is cleansed, Hebrews 9:14, and the Spirit is given to those who trust Him. Paul writes that anyone in Christ is a new creation, 2 Corinthians 5:17. God does what David asked: He creates a clean heart. The forgiven then become what David promised to be, teachers of the way to transgressors, Matthew 28:19-20.

The end of the story is a creation made new. Isaiah 65:17 uses the verb bara for the new heavens and the new earth, the same verb as David's request in verse 10. Every heart that was created clean in this age is a first fruit of that creation. In the new Jerusalem there will be no more need for cleansing, because the city will be free of what is unclean, Revelation 21:27, and the walls David prayed for will stand.

sermon.title: A Broken and Contrite Heart God Will Not Despise
sermon.why: Piper walks through David's downward spiral into sin and his four responses of repentance in this psalm, showing how Christ's atonement grounds the outrageous mercy God shows David, and how every believer today lays hold of that same mercy by turning to Christ, praying for cleansing, confessing the depth of sin, and pleading for renewal.

quiz.q: What is the historical occasion of this psalm, according to its heading?

options.text: David wrote it after Nathan the prophet confronted him over his adultery with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah.
options.note: This is stated directly in the psalm's heading and matches the events of 2 Samuel 11-12.

options.text: David wrote it while hiding from Saul in a cave.
options.note: That setting belongs to other psalms, such as Psalm 57, not this one.

options.text: David wrote it after his victory over Goliath.
options.note: This psalm is a penitential prayer over grave sin, not a victory song.

options.text: David wrote it during his coronation as king.
options.note: The psalm's entire tone is one of confession and repentance, not celebration of enthronement.

quiz.q: In verse 4, why does David say his sin is 'against You, You only'?

options.text: Because what makes sin truly sinful is that it is ultimately an offense against God, even though it deeply harmed others too.
options.note: This does not deny the real harm to Bathsheba, Uriah, and others; it identifies the deepest dimension of sin as an offense against God.

options.text: Because Bathsheba and Uriah were not actually harmed by his actions.
options.note: This directly contradicts the historical record; both were gravely harmed, and Uriah was killed.

options.text: Because human sin can never truly affect other people, only God.
options.note: Scripture consistently teaches sin harms others; the verse is about sin's deepest nature, not a denial of human harm.

options.text: Because David believed no human authority had the right to judge a king.
options.note: The point of the verse is theological, about the nature of sin itself, not a claim about royal immunity from human judgment.

quiz.q: What is David's central request in verse 10, and why is it significant?

options.text: Create in me a clean heart, using the same Hebrew verb, bara, as God's creation from nothing in Genesis 1:1.
options.note: This shows David is not asking for mere reform but for an entirely new creation within him.

options.text: Give me a new house to live in.
options.note: The request is for inner spiritual renewal, not material provision.

options.text: Restore my kingdom and my throne.
options.note: The psalm's concern is inner cleansing and renewal, not political restoration.

options.text: Teach me to avoid future temptation through willpower alone.
options.note: David asks God to create something new in him, not merely to strengthen his own willpower.

quiz.q: According to verses 16-17, what does God ultimately desire more than sacrifice?

options.text: A broken spirit and a contrite heart.
options.note: Verse 17 states this explicitly as what God will not despise.

options.text: Larger and costlier sacrifices than before.
options.note: The text says the opposite; God does not delight in sacrifice or burnt offerings for their own sake here.

options.text: Public displays of royal wealth.
options.note: This is not mentioned; the emphasis is entirely on inward brokenness before God.

options.text: A vow of silence.
options.note: David in fact vows to teach and sing praise, not to remain silent; the emphasis is on a broken and contrite heart.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's plea for a clean heart find its fulfillment in the New Testament?

options.text: In the new covenant promise of a new heart and God's own Spirit within His people, fulfilled in the new birth Jesus describes in John 3.
options.note: Ezekiel 36:26-27 and John 3:3-8 directly answer David's plea for a clean heart and a right spirit.

options.text: In the teaching that no one can ever truly be made clean before God.
options.note: This contradicts the entire thrust of the gospel, that Christ's blood does cleanse believers.

options.text: In the abolition of the need for repentance altogether.
options.note: The New Testament continues to call believers to ongoing confession and repentance, 1 John 1:9.

options.text: In a purely future hope with no present experience of renewal.
options.note: Scripture teaches believers experience real, present renewal now through the Spirit, not merely a future hope.

questions: David confesses honestly without excuse, appealing only to God's steadfast love. Where do you tend to minimize, excuse, or hide your sin rather than confessing it as plainly as David does here?
David asks not merely for forgiveness but for God to create in him a clean heart. Are you seeking only relief from guilt, or are you also asking God to change the desires beneath your sin?

Notably, David never asks God for more willpower against temptation; he asks for the joy of God's salvation to be restored. How might chasing joy in God, rather than mere self-control, change the way you fight a particular temptation?
David says God does not delight in sacrifice divorced from a broken and contrite heart. Where might you be relying on religious activity to cover over an unrepentant heart?
David resolves that once restored, he will teach transgressors and sinners will return to God. How might your own history of sin and grace equip you to help someone else who is struggling right now?

translationNotes.note: Brought forth in iniquity does not excuse David's specific sin by blaming his birth; rather, it intensifies his confession, showing that his adultery and murder were fruit of a deeper, inborn corruption rather than isolated, uncharacteristic acts.
Hyssop was the branch priests used to sprinkle blood for ceremonial cleansing, Leviticus 14:4-7; David appeals to God as his true priest to declare him clean.
Create renders bara, the same verb used only of God's activity in Genesis 1:1, implying David asks not for repair or improvement but for something entirely new.
